title: Standard error of a proportion: dependency on true proportion p
scenario_markdown: A polling and public opinion research firm designs two statewide probability surveys, each with sample size $n = 400$. In Survey A (a hotly contested referendum), the true population support is closely split near $p_A = 0.50$. In Survey B (household ownership of premium electric vehicles), the true population adoption is low, near $p_B = 0.10$.
assumptions: Independent random sampling of respondents without replacement from a large state population
Sampling fraction is under 5%, so FPC factor is not required
Success-failure conditions are met: for Survey A, np = 200 >= 10 and n(1-p) = 200 >= 10; for Survey B, np = 40 >= 10 and n(1-p) = 360 >= 10
source_refs: Course Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Confidence Intervals

approval.notes: Verified mathematical derivations: Survey A SE = sqrt(0.50 * 0.50 / 400) = sqrt(0.25 / 400) = 0.025 (2.50%). Survey B SE = sqrt(0.10 * 0.90 / 400) = sqrt(0.09 / 400) = 0.015 (1.50%). Ratio of standard errors = 0.025 / 0.015 = 5/3 approx 1.667. Proved quadratic peak of p(1-p) at p = 0.50. Excel formulas: =SQRT(0.50*0.50/400) and =SQRT(0.10*0.90/400).

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the standard error $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ for Survey A with $n = 400$ and $p_A = 0.50$.

options.hint_markdown: This is the sampling variance $\frac{p(1-p)}{n} = \frac{0.25}{400} = 0.000625$; you must take the square root $\sqrt{0.000625} = 0.025$.
Do not divide $p(1-p) = 0.25$ by $\sqrt{n} = 20$; the entire fraction $\frac{p(1-p)}{n}$ is under the square root.
Remember the complement term $(1 - p)$: $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$, not $\sqrt{\frac{p}{n}}$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the standard error $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ for Survey B with the same sample size $n = 400$ but $p_B = 0.10$.

options.text_markdown: $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = 0.025$ ($2.50\%$, because both surveys have identical sample size $n = 400$)
options.hint_markdown: Unlike the sample mean where $\sigma$ is fixed, the standard error of a proportion directly depends on the true proportion $p$ through $p(1-p)$.
Remember to take the square root of the variance: $\sqrt{0.000225} = 0.015$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Why is the standard error of Survey A ($0.025$) notably higher than that of Survey B ($0.015$) despite using identical sample sizes ($n = 400$)?

options.text_markdown: The product $p(1-p)$ describes a downward parabola reaching its maximum at $p = 0.50$, so estimation uncertainty is highest when a population is evenly split.
Extreme or rare proportions have greater statistical variability because rare events are harder to observe.
options.hint_markdown: When $p$ is close to 0 or 1, most outcomes are identical, so Bernoulli variability $p(1-p)$ is actually very small (e.g., $0.10 \times 0.90 = 0.09$ vs $0.50 \times 0.50 = 0.25$).

options.text_markdown: Survey B violates the Central Limit Theorem because $p = 0.10$ is too small for a normal approximation.
options.hint_markdown: For Survey B, $np = 400(0.10) = 40 \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) = 400(0.90) = 360 \ge 10$, so the normal approximation is fully satisfied.

options.text_markdown: A sample size of $n = 400$ is biased when surveying split opinions.
options.hint_markdown: Sample proportion $\hat{p}$ is an unbiased estimator ($E[\hat{p}] = p$) regardless of whether $p = 0.5$ or $p = 0.1$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The Bernoulli variance term $p(1-p) = p - p^2$ has its derivative $1 - 2p = 0$, giving a strict global maximum at $p = 0.50$ where $p(1-p) = 0.25$. When $p = 0.10$, $p(1-p) = 0.09$, which is less than $36\%$ of the variance at $p = 0.50$. Consequently, public opinion polls face the largest sampling variability and margin of error when the electorate is evenly split ($50/50$). This is why conservative sample size planning assumes $p = 0.50$ when no prior estimate is available.
